translations.text: In my first book, Theophilus, I wrote about everything that our Lord Jesus Christ began to do and teach,
until the day he was taken up, after he had given instructions to the apostles whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit.
After his suffering, he also showed himself alive to them by many signs over forty days, appearing to them and speaking about the kingdom of God.
While he was eating bread with them, he commanded them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the Father's promise: “The promise you heard about from me.
For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit in a few days.”
When they were gathered together, they asked him, “Our Lord, are you restoring the kingdom to Israel at this time?”
He said to them, “It is not for you to know the time or the seasons that the Father has established by his own authority.
But when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, throughout Judea, also in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”
After he said these things, he was taken up while they watched him. A cloud received him, and he was hidden from their eyes.
While they were looking up into heaven as he went, two men in white clothing appeared standing beside them.
They said to them, “Men of Galilee, why are you standing and looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way that you saw him go up into heaven.”
Afterward they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called the Mount of Olives, which is near Jerusalem, about seven stadia away.

After they entered, they went up to the upstairs room where they were staying: Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Matthew and Bartholomew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James.
All of them devoted themselves together to prayer with one mind, along with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.
In those days Simon Peter stood up among the disciples. There was a gathering of about a hundred and twenty people there, and he said:
“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled that the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus.
For he was counted among us and had a share in this ministry.
He acquired a field with the payment for his sin. He fell face down on the ground, split open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out.
This became known to everyone living in Jerusalem, and so that field was called Akeldama in the local language, which means ‘Field of Blood.’
For it is written in the book of Psalms: ‘Let his dwelling become desolate, and let no one live in it,’ and, ‘Let someone else take his ministry.’
Therefore, one of these men who were with us throughout the whole time that our Lord Jesus came and went among us,
beginning with John's baptism until the day he was taken up from us, must become a witness with us to his resurrection.”
They put forward two men: Joseph, called Barsabbas, who was also named Justus, and Matthias.
They prayed and said, “You, Lord, know what is in everyone's heart. Show which one of these two you have chosen,
That he may receive a share in this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas departed to go to his own place.
They cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
When the days of Pentecost had come, while they were all gathered together,
suddenly a sound came from heaven like a powerful wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting.
Tongues appeared to them, dividing like fire, and settled on each one of them.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began speaking in various languages, as the Spirit enabled them to speak.
Now there were men living in Jerusalem who feared God, Jews from every nation under heaven.
When that sound came, all the people gathered and were bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in their own languages.
They were all astonished and amazed, saying to one another, “Aren't all these people who are speaking Galileans?
How is it that each of us hears our own native language?
Parthians, Medes, and Alans; those who live in Mesopotamia; Jews and Cappadocians; and those from the region of Pontus and Asia.
And those from the regions of Phrygia and Pamphylia, from Egypt and the regions of Libya near Cyrene, and those who came from Rome, both Jews and converts to Judaism.
And those from Crete, and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own languages about the wonders of God.
They were all amazed and bewildered, saying to one another, “What does this mean?”
But others mocked them, saying, “These people have drunk sweet wine and become drunk.”
Then Simon Peter stood up with the eleven apostles, raised his voice, and said to them, “Jewish men and everyone living in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words.
For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day.
Rather, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel:
“In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, and your old men will dream dreams.
Even on my male servants and my female servants I will pour out my Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy.
I will give signs in heaven and mighty wonders on earth: blood and fire and clouds of smoke.
The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and fearsome day of the Lord comes.
And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will live.”
Men of Israel, listen to these words: Jesus of Nazareth was a man whom God made known to you through miracles, signs, and mighty wonders that God did among you through him, as you yourselves know.
This man, who had been set apart for this by God's foreknowledge and will, you handed over into the hands of wicked men, and you crucified and killed him.
But God raised him up and released him from the pains of Sheol, because it was impossible for him to be held in Sheol.
For David said about him, “I always saw my Lord before me, for he is at my right hand so that I will not be shaken.
Therefore my heart was glad, and my glory rejoiced; my body too will rest in hope.
For you will not abandon my soul in Sheol, nor will you let your Holy One see decay.
You have revealed to me the path of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence.
Brothers, I may speak openly to you about the patriarch David: he died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day.
For he was a prophet, and he knew that God had sworn oaths to him: “I will seat one of your descendants on your throne.”
He foresaw this and spoke about the resurrection of the Messiah: he was not abandoned in Sheol, nor did his body see decay.
God raised this Jesus, and we are all his witnesses.
He is the one who was exalted at God's right hand and received from the Father the promise concerning the Holy Spirit. He poured out this gift, which you now see and hear.
For it was not David who ascended to heaven, since he himself said, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’”
Until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.
Therefore let the whole house of Israel know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Messiah.
When they heard these things, they were deeply distressed in their hearts and said to Simon and the rest of the apostles, “What should we do, brothers?”
Simon said to them, “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus for the forgiveness of sins, so that you may receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
For the promise is for you and your children, and for all who are far away, those whom God himself will call.”
With many other words he testified to them and pleaded with them, saying, “Be saved from this crooked generation.”
Some of them readily accepted his message, believed, and were baptized. About three thousand people were added that day.
They remained devoted to the apostles' teaching and shared together in prayer and in the breaking of the Eucharist.
Awe came upon everyone, and many signs and mighty deeds were being done through the apostles in Jerusalem.
All those who believed were together, and everything they had was held in common.
Those who owned property sold it and distributed it to each person according to what they needed.
Every day they continued together in the temple with one accord. At home they broke bread and ate their food with joy and sincerity of heart,
praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. Every day our Lord added to the church those who were being saved.
Now Simon Peter and John were going up together to the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer,

and there was a man, lame from his mother's womb, being carried by people who regularly brought him and placed him at the temple gate called Beautiful, so that he could ask for alms from those entering the temple.
When he saw Simon and John going into the temple, he asked them to give him alms.
Simon and John looked intently at him and said to him, “Look at us.”
He looked at them, expecting to receive something from them.
Simon said to him, “I have no gold or silver, but what I do have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk.”
He took him by his right hand and helped him up. Immediately his feet and ankles became strong.
He jumped up, stood, and walked. He entered the temple with them, walking and jumping and praising God.
All the people saw him walking and praising God.
They recognized him as the beggar who used to sit every day asking for charity at the gate called Beautiful. They were filled with amazement and wonder at what had happened.
While he was holding on to Simon and John, all the people ran to them in amazement, to the portico called Solomon’s.
When Simon saw this, he said to them, “Men of Israel, why are you amazed at this? Or why are you staring at us, as though we had made this man walk by our own power or authority?”
The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our ancestors, glorified his Son Jesus, whom you handed over and disowned before Pilate, even though he had decided to release him.
But you disowned the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be given to you.
You killed the leader of life, whom God raised from the dead. We are all his witnesses.
Through faith in his name, he has strengthened and healed this man whom you see and know. Faith in him has given this man this complete health in front of you all.
But now, my brothers, I know that you did this in ignorance, as your rulers also did.
In this way God fulfilled what he had announced beforehand through all the prophets: that his Messiah would suffer.
Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away and times of relief may come to you from the presence of the Lord.
And he will send you the one who was prepared for you, Jesus Christ.
Heaven must receive him until the fulfillment of the times of all the things that God spoke of through his holy prophets from long ago.
For Moses said, “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. Listen to him in everything he tells you.
And every person who does not listen to that prophet will be destroyed from among their people.”
All the prophets, from Samuel onward, including those who came after him, spoke and proclaimed those days.
You are the children of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with our ancestors when he said to Abraham, “Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.”
God raised up his Son and sent him to you first, to bless you if you turn back and repent of your evil deeds.
While they were speaking these words to the people, the priests, the Sadducees, and the temple officials came against them.
They were angry with them because they were teaching the people and proclaiming, in Christ, the resurrection from the dead.
They arrested them and held them until the next day, because evening was approaching.
Many who had heard the message believed, and their number was about five thousand men.
The next day, the rulers, elders, and scribes gathered together,
along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and those who belonged to the family of the high priests.
When they had made them stand in the middle, they asked them, “By what power or in what name did you do this?”
Then Simon Peter was filled with the Holy Spirit and said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders of the house of Israel, listen.
If you are judging us today over the good done to a sick man, asking how this man was healed,

let this be known to you and to all the people of Israel: it is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands here before you in good health.
He is the stone that you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.
There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to human beings by which we must live.”
When they heard how openly Simon and John spoke, they realized that they were uneducated, ordinary men, and they were amazed at them. They recognized them as men who had been with Jesus.
They saw the lame man who had been healed standing with them, and they could find nothing to say against them.
Then they ordered them to leave their assembly and said to one another,
“What should we do with these men? A clear sign has been performed through them, and it has become known to everyone living in Jerusalem. We cannot deny it.
But to keep this news from spreading any further among the people, let us threaten them so that they no longer speak to anyone in this name.”
They called them in and ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
Simon Peter and John answered them, “Judge for yourselves whether it is right before God to listen to you rather than to God.
For we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
They threatened them and released them, for they could find no charge to bring against them because of the people, since everyone was praising God for what had happened.
For the man in whom this sign of healing had taken place was over forty years old.
When they were released, they went to their brothers and told them everything the priests and elders had said.
When they heard this, they raised their voices together to God and said, “Lord, you are the God who made heaven and earth, the seas, and everything in them.
You are the one who spoke through the Holy Spirit by the mouth of your servant David: ‘Why did the peoples rage, and the nations devise empty plans?
The kings of the earth and the rulers rose up and took counsel together against the Lord and against his Anointed One.’
For truly, Herod and Pilate, together with the nations and the assembly of Israel, gathered in this city against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed,
to do everything that your hand and your will had determined beforehand would happen.
And now, Lord, look and see their threats, and grant that your servants may proclaim your word openly and boldly,
while you stretch out your hand for healings, mighty works, and signs to take place in the name of your holy Son Jesus.
When they had prayed and pleaded, the place where they were gathered was shaken. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God openly and boldly.
The whole community of those who believed had one soul and one mind. None of them said that any of the possessions they owned were their own, but everything they had was held in common.
With great power the apostles testified to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, and great grace was with them all.
There was no one among them in need, for those who owned fields and houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold,
and laid them at the apostles’ feet. They were distributed to each person according to what that person needed.
Now Joseph, whom the apostles had named Barnabas, which means “son of consolation,” was a Levite from the land of Cyprus.
He owned a field and sold it, brought its proceeds, and laid them at the apostles’ feet.
A man named Ananias, together with his wife, whose name was Sapphira, sold his field.
He took some of its price and hid it, with his wife’s knowledge. He brought part of the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
Simon said to him, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart like this, so that you would lie to the Holy Spirit and hide some of the money from the sale of the field?

Was it not yours before it was sold? And after it was sold, did you not still have control over its price? Why did you decide in your heart to do this thing? You have not lied to human beings, but to God.”
When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and died. Great fear came over everyone who heard.
The younger men among them got up, wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him.
After three hours had passed, his wife also came in, not knowing what had happened.
Simon said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the field for this amount.” She said, “Yes, for that amount.”
Simon said to her, “Because you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord, look—the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.”
Immediately she fell down at their feet and died. Those young men came in and found her dead. They wrapped her up, carried her away, and buried her beside her husband.
Great fear came over the whole church and over everyone who heard.
Many signs and mighty works were taking place among the people through the apostles. They were all gathered together in Solomon’s Portico.
None of the other people dared to approach them, but the people held them in high regard.
And more and more people who believed in the Lord were being added, a multitude of men and women,
People even brought the sick out into the streets, lying on beds, so that when Simon came by, at least his shadow might fall on them.
Many people also came to them from other towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those who had unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
The high priest and all those with him, who belonged to the teaching of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy.
They laid hands on the apostles, seized them, and locked them up in prison.
Then, during the night, an angel of the Lord opened the prison door, brought them out, and said to them,
“Go, stand in the temple and tell the people all these words of life.”

They went out at dawn, entered the temple, and began teaching. Meanwhile, the high priest and those with him called together their companions and the elders of Israel, and sent to the prison to have the apostles brought.
When those they had sent went there, they did not find them in the prison. They came back,
saying, “We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened it, we found no one there.”
When the chief priests and the temple officials heard these words, they were bewildered about them and wondered what this meant.
Someone came and told them, “Look! The men you locked up in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.”
Then the officials went with the guards to bring them, but without force, for they were afraid that the people might stone them.
When they had brought them, they stood them before the whole assembly, and the high priest proceeded to speak to them.
“Did we not strictly command you not to teach anyone in this name? Yet look, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you want to bring this man’s blood upon us.”
Simon, together with the apostles, answered them, “We must obey God rather than human beings.
The God of our ancestors raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree.
God appointed this very man as leader and Savior and exalted him by his right hand, to give Israel repentance and forgiveness of sins.
We are witnesses to these things, as is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who believe in him.”
When they heard these words, they were inflamed with anger and were considering killing them.
One of the Pharisees, named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law who was respected by all the people, stood up and ordered that the apostles be taken outside for a little while.
He said to them, “Men of Israel, be careful and consider what you ought to do about these men.
Before this time, Theudas rose up, claiming to be someone great, and about four hundred men followed him. He was killed, and those who had followed him were scattered and came to nothing.

After him, Judas the Galilean rose up in the days when people were being registered for the poll tax, and he led many people astray after him. He too died, and all those who had followed him were scattered.
And now I tell you: keep away from these men and leave them alone. For if this plan and this work are of human origin, they will fall apart and pass away.
But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop it. You may even find yourselves standing against God.
They were persuaded by him. They called in the apostles and flogged them, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them.
They left their presence rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the Name.
And every day, in the temple and at home, they never stopped teaching and proclaiming the good news about our Lord Jesus Christ.
In those days, as the disciples increased in number, the Greek-speaking disciples complained against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily service.
The twelve apostles called together the whole gathering of disciples and said to them, “It is not right for us to leave the word of God to serve tables.
So, my brothers, look carefully and choose seven men from among you who have a good reputation and are full of the Spirit of the Lord and wisdom, and we will put them in charge of this task.
But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.”
This proposal pleased all the people. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicholas, a convert to Judaism from Antioch.
These men stood before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
The word of God continued to spread, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem grew greatly. A large number of Jews became obedient to the faith.
Stephen was full of grace and power, and he performed signs and wonders among the people.
Some men from the synagogue called the Synagogue of the Freedmen rose up, along with Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and people from Cilicia and Asia, and they debated with Stephen.
But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit that spoke through him.
Then they sent men and coached them to say, “We heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and against God.”
They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes. They came and confronted him, seized him, and brought him into the midst of the council.
They brought forward false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking against the law and against this holy place.
For we heard him say that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to you.”
All those sitting in the council looked intently at him and saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
The high priest asked him whether these things were so.
He said, “Men, our brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia, before he came to live in Haran.
And he said to him, “Leave your land and your relatives, and come to the land that I will show you.”
Then Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and came to live in Haran. From there, after his father died, God moved him to this land where you live today.
He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a place to set his foot. But he promised to give it to him as a possession, to him and his descendants, even though he had no son.
God spoke with him and said, “Your descendants will live as foreigners in a foreign land, and they will enslave them and mistreat them for four hundred years.
But I will judge the nation they serve as slaves,” God said. “After these things, they will come out and serve me in this place.”
And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. Then he fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day. Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob fathered our twelve ancestors.
Our ancestors were jealous of Joseph and sold him into Egypt. But God was with him.
He rescued him from all his troubles and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Pharaoh appointed him ruler over Egypt and over his entire household.
There was a famine and great distress throughout Egypt and the land of Canaan, and our ancestors did not have enough to eat.
When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our ancestors there for the first time.
When they went a second time, Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh.
Joseph sent for his father Jacob and brought him and his entire family. They numbered seventy-five people.
Jacob went down to Egypt, and he died there, as did our ancestors.
He was moved to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought with silver from the sons of Hamor.
As the time approached for what God had promised Abraham under oath, the people increased in number and grew strong in Egypt,
until another king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph.
He dealt cunningly with our people and mistreated our ancestors. He ordered that their newborn children be thrown out so that they would not survive.
At that time Moses was born, and he was loved by God. He was brought up for three months in his father’s house.
When he was thrown out by his mother, Pharaoh’s daughter found him and raised him as her own son.
Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was capable in both his words and his deeds.
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the Israelites.
He saw one of his own people being treated harshly, so he defended him and secured justice for him. He killed the Egyptian who was wronging him.
He thought that his brothers, the Israelites, understood that God was giving them deliverance through him, but they did not understand.
The next day he appeared among them as they were fighting with one another. He tried to persuade them to make peace, saying, “Men, you are brothers. Why are you wronging one another?”
But the one who was wronging his companion pushed him away and said to him, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?
Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?”
Moses fled because of this matter and became a foreign resident in the land of Midian. There he had two sons.
When forty years had passed for him there, the angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a fire burning in a bush.
When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight. As he approached to look, the Lord spoke to him aloud:
“I am the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” Moses trembled and did not dare to look at the sight.
The Lord said to him, “Take your sandals off your feet, for the ground on which you are standing is holy.
I have certainly seen the suffering of my people in Egypt and have heard their groans. I have come down to rescue them. Now come, and I will send you to Egypt.”
This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?”—this very man God sent to them as ruler and deliverer through the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
He was the one who led them out, performing signs, wonders, and mighty deeds in the land of Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own people. Listen to him.”
He was the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness, with the angel who spoke with him and with our ancestors on Mount Sinai. He was the one who received living words to give to us.
Our ancestors were unwilling to obey him. Instead, they abandoned him and turned back to Egypt in their hearts.
They said to Aaron, “Make us gods to go before us, because we do not know what has happened to this Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt.”
In those days they made themselves a calf and offered sacrifices to idols. They delighted in the work of their own hands.

God turned away and handed them over to worship the heavenly hosts, as it is written in the book of the prophets: “Did you offer me slaughtered animals or sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, people of Israel?”
Instead, you carried the tent of Milcom and the star of the god Rephan, images you made to worship. I will deport you beyond Babylon.
Look, our ancestors had the tent of testimony in the wilderness, just as the one who spoke with Moses commanded him to make it according to the pattern he showed him.
Our ancestors also brought this tent with Joshua into the land that God gave them as an inheritance from the nations he drove out before them. It was passed down until the days of David,
who found favor before God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.
But Solomon built him a house.
Yet the Most High does not dwell in things made by human hands, as the prophet said:
“Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool beneath my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or where is the place for me to rest?
Did not my own hand make all these things?”
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and hearing! You always resist the Holy Spirit. You are just like your ancestors.
For which of the prophets did your ancestors not persecute and kill—those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, whom you betrayed and killed?
You received the law through the command of angels, but you did not keep it.
When they heard these things, they were filled with rage and gnashed their teeth at him.
But he, full of faith and the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at God's right hand.
He said, "Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand."
They shouted loudly, covered their ears, and all threatened him.
They seized him, took him outside the city, and began stoning him. Those who had testified against him laid their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul.
They were stoning Stephen as he prayed and said, "Our Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
He knelt down and cried out loudly, "Our Lord, do not hold this sin against them." When he had said this, he fell asleep.

Saul approved and shared in his killing. That day a great persecution arose against the church in Jerusalem, and everyone except the apostles was scattered throughout the villages of Judea and the territory of the Samaritans.
Faithful men gathered up Stephen and buried him, and they mourned deeply for him.
But Saul was persecuting God's church, entering houses, dragging away men and women, and handing them over to prison.
Those who had been scattered traveled about, proclaiming the word of God.
Philip went down to the city of the Samaritans and proclaimed the Messiah to them.
When the people there heard his message, they listened to him and were persuaded by everything he said, because they saw the signs he was performing.
For many who were possessed by unclean spirits cried out loudly, and the spirits came out of them. Others who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
There was great joy in that city.
There was a man there named Simon who had lived in the city for a long time. Through his sorcery he led the Samaritan people astray, exalting himself and saying, "I am someone great."
Everyone, great and small, turned to him and said, "This man is the great power of God."
They were all persuaded by him because he had amazed them with his sorcery for a long time.
But when they believed Philip, who was proclaiming the good news of God's kingdom, men and women were baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Simon himself also believed and was baptized, and he stayed close to Philip. When he saw the signs and great miracles taking place through him, he was amazed and astonished.
When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that the Samaritan people had accepted the word of God, they sent Simon Peter and John to them.
They went down and prayed for them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit.
For he had not yet come upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
When Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,
saying, “Give me this authority too, so that anyone on whom I lay my hand may receive the Holy Spirit.”
Simon Peter said to him, “May your money perish with you, because you thought that God’s gift could be bought with worldly wealth.
You have no part or share in this faith, because your heart is not right before God.
But repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to God, so that perhaps the deceit in your heart may be forgiven you.
For I see that you are in bitter gall and in the bonds of wickedness.”
Simon answered, “Pray to God for me yourselves, so that none of the things you have said may come upon me.”
After Simon and John had testified to them and taught the word of God, they returned to Jerusalem. They proclaimed the good news in many villages of the Samaritans.
An angel of the Lord spoke with Philip and said to him, “Get up and go south along the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.”
He got up and went. He encountered a eunuch who had come from Cush, an official of Candace, queen of the Cushites. He was in charge of her entire treasury and had come to worship in Jerusalem.
As he was returning home, he was sitting in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and stay close to the chariot.”
As he approached, he heard him reading the prophet Isaiah and said to him, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
He said, “How can I understand unless someone guides me?” He asked Philip to come up and sit with him.
The passage of Scripture he was reading was this: “Like a lamb he was led to slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearer he was silent. In the same way, he did not open his mouth[?].
In his humiliation he was led away from imprisonment and judgment. Who can recount his generation? For his life is taken from the earth.”
The eunuch said to Philip, “Please tell me, about whom did the prophet say this—about himself or about someone else?”
Then Philip opened his mouth and, beginning with this Scripture, proclaimed to him the good news about our Lord Jesus.
As they traveled along the road, they came to a place where there was water. The eunuch said, “Look, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?”
Philip said, “If you believe with all your heart, it is permitted.” He answered, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”
He ordered the chariot to stop. Both of them went down into the water, and Philip baptized the eunuch.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again. But he went on his way rejoicing.
Philip was found at Azotus. From there he traveled around, proclaiming the good news in all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
Saul, meanwhile, was still full of threats and murderous rage against the disciples of our Lord.
He asked the high priest to give him letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found anyone following this Way, whether men or women, he could bind them and bring them to Jerusalem.
As he traveled and began to approach Damascus, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.”
He answered, “Who are you, my Lord?” Our Lord said, “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.
But get up and enter the city, and there you will be told what you must do.”
The men traveling with him stood amazed, because they heard only the voice but could see no one.
Saul got up from the ground, but he could see nothing, although his eyes were open. They took him by the hands and led him into Damascus.
For three days he could not see, and he neither ate nor drank.
There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Here I am, my Lord.”
Our Lord said to him, “Get up and go to the street called Straight, and at Judas’s house ask for Saul, who is from the city of Tarsus. For look, while he is praying,
he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hand on him so that his eyes might be opened.”
Ananias said, “My Lord, I have heard from many people about this man and how much harm he has made your holy people suffer in Jerusalem.”
“And look, even here he has authority from the chief priests to arrest everyone who calls on your name.”
The Lord said to him, “Get up and go, because he is my chosen instrument to carry my name among the nations and kings and the people of Israel.
For I will show him how much he is to suffer for my name.”

Then Ananias went to him at the house, laid his hand on him, and said to him, “Saul, my brother, our Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming, has sent me so that your eyes might be opened and you might be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and his eyes were opened. He got up and was baptized.
He ate some food and regained his strength. He stayed for several days with the disciples who were in Damascus.
Immediately he began proclaiming in the Jewish synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

Everyone who heard him was amazed and said, “Isn’t this the man who persecuted everyone who called on this name in Jerusalem? And wasn’t he sent here for this very purpose, to arrest them and bring them to the chief priests?”
But Saul grew stronger and stronger, and he confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by demonstrating that Jesus is the Messiah.
After he had spent many days there, the Jews plotted to kill him.
But Saul learned of the plot they intended to carry out against him. They were watching the city gates day and night to kill him.
Then the disciples put him in a basket and lowered him from the wall at night.
He went to Jerusalem and wanted to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him and did not believe that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles. He told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road, how the Lord had spoken to him, and how he had spoken openly in Damascus in the name of Jesus.
He went in and out with them in Jerusalem.
He spoke openly in the name of Jesus and debated with the Jews who knew Greek. But they wanted to kill him.
When the brothers learned of this, they brought him to Caesarea by night, and from there they sent him to Tarsus.
Meanwhile, the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace. It was being built up and was walking in the fear of God, and it grew through the encouragement of the Holy Spirit.
As Simon traveled around the towns, he also went down to the saints who lived in the town of Lydda.
He found a man named Aeneas who had been bedridden and paralyzed for eight years.
Simon said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed.” Immediately he got up.
Everyone who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to God.
In the town of Joppa there was a female disciple named Tabitha. She was rich in good deeds and in the charitable gifts she gave.
During those days she became sick and died. They washed her and laid her in an upstairs room.
The disciples had heard that Simon was in the town of Lydda, which is near Joppa. They sent two men to him to ask him not to hesitate to come to them.

Simon got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him up to the upstairs room. All the widows gathered and stood around him, weeping and showing him the tunics and cloaks that Tabitha had given them while she was alive.
Simon sent everyone outside, knelt down, and prayed. Then he turned toward the body and said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Simon, she sat up.
He held out his hand to her and helped her stand. Then he called the saints and the widows and presented her to them alive.
This became known throughout the town, and many believed in our Lord.
He stayed in Joppa for many days, lodging at the house of Simon the tanner.
In Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion from the regiment called the Italian Regiment.
He was righteous and feared God, along with his entire household. He gave many charitable gifts to the people and prayed to God continually.
At about three in the afternoon, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God come in to him and say, “Cornelius!”
He stared at him in fear and said, “What is it, my lord?” The angel said to him, “Your prayers and your charitable gifts have risen as a memorial before God.
Now send men to the town of Joppa and bring Simon, who is called Peter.
He is staying at the house of Simon the tanner, by the sea.”
When the angel who had spoken with him left, he called two members of his household and a God-fearing soldier who attended him.
He told them everything he had seen and sent them to Joppa.
The next day, while they were traveling along the road and approaching the city, Simon went up to the roof to pray at noon.
He became hungry and wanted to eat. While they were preparing food for him, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven opened and a container tied at its four corners. It looked like a large linen sheet and was being lowered from heaven to the earth.
In it were all kinds of four-footed animals, creatures that crawl on the ground, and birds of the sky.
A voice came to him, saying, “Simon, get up, slaughter and eat.”
Simon said, “Certainly not, my Lord! I have never eaten anything defiled or unclean.”
Again, a second time, a voice came to him: “What God has made clean, you must not treat as defiled.”
This happened three times, and the container was lifted up to heaven.

While Simon was wondering to himself what the vision he had seen meant, the men sent by Cornelius arrived. They asked about the house where Simon was staying, then came and stood at the courtyard gate.
They called out there and asked whether Simon, who was called Peter, was staying there.
While Simon was thinking about the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Look, three men are looking for you.
Get up, go downstairs, and go with them without any hesitation, because I myself have sent them.”
Then Simon went down to those men and said to them, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason you have come?”

They said to him, “A man named Cornelius, a righteous centurion who fears God and is well spoken of by the whole Jewish people, was told in a vision by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear a message from you.”
Simon brought them inside and welcomed them where he was staying. The next day he got up and went away with them. Some of the brothers from Joppa also went with him.
The following day he entered Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having gathered all his relatives and his close friends.
As Simon was entering, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet in worship.
Simon raised him up and said to him, “Stand up. I too am a human being.”
As he talked with him, he went inside and found many people who had come there.
He said to them, “You know that a Jewish man is not permitted to associate with a foreigner who is not one of his own people. But God has shown me that I must not call anyone unclean or defiled.
That is why I came readily when you sent for me. But I ask you: why did you send for me?”
Cornelius said to him, “It has now been four days since I began fasting. At three in the afternoon, while I was praying in my house, a man dressed in white stood before me.
He said to me, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your gifts to the poor have been remembered before God.
Now send to the city of Joppa and bring Simon, who is called Peter. He is staying at the house of Simon the tanner, beside the sea. He will come and speak with you.’
I sent for you immediately, and you have done well to come. Now we are all here before you, and we want to hear everything that God has commanded you.”
Then Simon opened his mouth and said, “I truly understand that God shows no partiality.
But in every nation, anyone who fears him and does what is right is accepted by him.
For the message he sent to the people of Israel proclaimed to them peace and harmony through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all.
You yourselves know about what happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed,
concerning Jesus of Nazareth: God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went around healing those who had been harmed by the evil one, because God was with him.
We are his witnesses to everything he did throughout the land of Judea and in Jerusalem. The Jews hung this man on a tree and killed him.
God raised him on the third day and allowed him to be plainly seen,
not by all the people, but by us whom God chose to be his witnesses, who ate and drank with him after his resurrection from the dead.
He commanded us to proclaim and testify to the people that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.
All the prophets testified about him that everyone who believes in his name will receive forgiveness of sins.”
While Simon was speaking these words, the Holy Spirit overshadowed everyone who was listening to the message.
The circumcised brothers who had come with him were amazed and astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the Gentiles too.
For they heard them speaking in various languages and magnifying God. Then Simon said,
“Can anyone withhold water so that these people cannot be baptized? Look, they have received the Holy Spirit just as we have.”
Then he commanded them to be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. They asked him to stay with them for some days.
The apostles and the brothers in Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.
When Simon went up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision disputed with him,
saying, “He went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them.”
Simon began explaining it to them step by step:
“While I was praying in Joppa, I saw in a vision something like a linen sheet coming down. It was tied at its four corners and was being lowered from heaven, and it came right to me.
I looked into it and saw that it contained four-footed animals, creatures that crawl on the ground, and birds of the sky.
I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Simon, get up, slaughter and eat.’
I said, ‘Certainly not, Lord! Nothing unclean or defiled has ever entered my mouth.’
Again a voice from heaven said to me, ‘What God has made clean, you must not treat as defiled.’
This happened three times, and everything was taken up into heaven.
At that very moment, three men sent to me by Cornelius from Caesarea arrived and stood at the gate of the house where I was staying.
The Spirit told me to go with them without hesitation. These six brothers also came with me, and we entered the man's house.
He told us how he had seen an angel standing in his house, who said to him, "Send to the city of Joppa and bring Simon, who is called Cephas."
He will speak words to you by which you and your entire household will live.
As I began speaking there, the Holy Spirit came upon them, just as upon us at the beginning.
Then I remembered the words of our Lord, who had said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’
So if God gave the gift equally to the Gentiles who believed in our Lord Jesus Christ, just as he did to us, who was I to be able to stand in God’s way?
When they heard these words, they became quiet and praised God, saying, ‘Then God has also granted the Gentiles repentance that leads to life.’
Now those who had been scattered by the persecution that arose over Stephen had reached as far as Phoenicia, the land of Cyprus, and Antioch. They spoke the word to no one except Jews.
But some of them were men from Cyprus and Cyrene. These came to Antioch and spoke to the Greeks, telling them the good news about our Lord Jesus.
The hand of the Lord was with them, and many believed and turned to the Lord.
News of this reached the members of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch.
When he arrived there and saw God’s grace, he rejoiced and urged them all to remain devoted to our Lord with their whole hearts,
because he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith. A great many people were added to our Lord.
He went to Tarsus to look for Saul.

When he found him, he brought him back with him to Antioch. For a whole year they gathered together in the church and taught a great many people. It was then, in Antioch, that the disciples were first called Christians.
In those days prophets came there from Jerusalem.
One of them, named Agabus, stood up and made known to them through the Spirit that a great famine would come upon the whole earth. This famine occurred in the days of Claudius Caesar.
So the disciples decided, each according to what he had, to send aid to the brothers living in Judea.
They sent it to the elders there through Barnabas and Saul.
At that time King Herod, who was called Agrippa, laid hands on some members of the church to mistreat them.
He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Simon Peter as well. These were the days of Unleavened Bread.
He arrested him and put him in prison, handing him over to sixteen soldiers to guard him, so that after Passover they would hand him over to the Jewish people.
While Simon was being held in prison, the church was continually offering prayer to God on his behalf.
On that very night, before he was to be handed over in the morning, Simon was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while others guarded the prison doors.
An angel of the Lord stood over him, and a light shone throughout the building. He struck him on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly!” And the chains fell from his hands.
The angel said to him, “Fasten your belt and put on your sandals.” He did so. Then he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.”
He went out and followed him, not knowing that what was happening through the angel was real, for he thought he was seeing a vision.
After they passed the first and second guard posts, they came to the iron gate, and it opened for them of its own accord. When they had gone out and passed along one street, the angel left him.
Then Simon came to his senses and said, “Now I know for certain that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the power of King Herod and from what the Jews were planning against me.”
When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was also called Mark, because many brothers were gathered there praying.
He knocked at the courtyard gate, and a girl named Rhoda came out to answer him.
She recognized Simon’s voice, but in her joy she did not open the gate for him. Instead, she ran back and told them, “Look, Simon is standing at the courtyard gate!”
They said to her, “You are out of your mind!” But she kept insisting that it was so. They said to her, “Perhaps it is his angel.”
Meanwhile, Simon kept knocking at the gate. They came out, saw him, and were amazed.

He motioned with his hand for them to be quiet. He went inside and told them how the Lord had brought him out of prison. Then he said to them, “Tell these things to James and our brothers.” And he left and went to another place.
When morning came, there was a great commotion among the soldiers over what had happened to Simon.
Herod searched for him but did not find him. He put the guards on trial and ordered them to be put to death. Then he left Judea and stayed in Caesarea.

Because he was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, they gathered and came to him together. They won over Blastus, the official in charge of the king’s bedroom, and asked him for peace, because their country’s food supply came from Herod’s kingdom.
On an appointed day, Herod put on royal clothing, sat on the judgment seat, and addressed the crowd.
All the people shouted, “These are the words of God, not of human beings!”
Because he did not give glory to God, the angel of the Lord struck him at that very moment. He became infested with worms and died.
And the good news of God continued to be proclaimed and to spread.
Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem to Antioch after completing their service. They took with them John, who was also called Mark.
Now in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas; Simeon, who was called Niger; Lucius from the city of Cyrene; Manaen, the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch; and Saul.
While they were fasting and praying earnestly to God, the Holy Spirit said to them, “Set apart Saul and Barnabas for me, for the work to which I have called them.”
After they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them away.
So, having been sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus.
When they entered the city of Salamis, they proclaimed the word of our Lord in the Jewish synagogues. John was serving as their assistant.
When they had traveled through the whole island as far as the city of Paphos, they found a Jewish sorcerer, a false prophet named Barshuma.
He was associated with an intelligent man named Sergius Paulus, who was the proconsul. The proconsul summoned Saul and Barnabas and wanted to hear the word of God from them.
But this sorcerer Barshuma, whose name is translated Elymas, opposed them, because he wanted to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
But Saul, who was called Paul, was filled with the Holy Spirit and looked intently at him.
He said, “You who are full of every kind of deceit and all wickedness, son of the devil and enemy of all righteousness! Will you not stop twisting the straight ways of the Lord?

Now the hand of the Lord is upon you. You will be blind and will not see the sun for a time.” Immediately, mist and darkness fell upon him, and he wandered about looking for someone to take him by the hand.
When the proconsul saw what had happened, he was amazed and believed in the teaching of the Lord.
Paul and Barnabas sailed from the city of Paphos and came to the city of Perga in Pamphylia. John left them and went to Jerusalem.
They left Perga and came to the city of Antioch in Pisidia. They entered the synagogue and sat down on the day [?] the Sabbath.
After the Law and the Prophets had been read, the elders of the synagogue sent word to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement, speak to the people.”
Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and said, "Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen."
The God of this people chose our ancestors and exalted them and made them great while they were foreigners in the land of Egypt. With an uplifted arm he brought them out of it.
He sustained them in the wilderness for forty years.
He destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan and gave them their land as an inheritance.
For four hundred and fifty years he gave them judges, until Samuel the prophet.
Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
He removed him and raised up David as their king. He testified about him, saying, “I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart. He will carry out all my wishes.”
From this man's descendants, God raised up Jesus as a Savior for Israel, as he had promised.
He sent John to proclaim a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel before Jesus' coming.
As John was finishing his ministry, he said, “Who do you think I am? I am not he. But look, someone is coming after me whose sandal straps I am not worthy to untie.”
Brothers, descendants of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, this message of life has been sent to you.

For the inhabitants of Jerusalem and their leaders did not recognize it, nor did they understand the writings of the prophets that are read every Sabbath. Instead, they condemned him and fulfilled what was written.
Although they found no grounds for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him killed.
When they had fulfilled everything written about him, they took him down from the cross and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead.
For many days he appeared to those who had gone up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now his witnesses to the people.
And we too are bringing you the good news that the promise made to our ancestors—
God has now fulfilled it for us, their children, by raising up Jesus, as it is written in the second psalm: “You are my Son; today I have fathered you.”
God raised him from the dead in such a way that he would never return to experience decay, as he said, “I will give you the unfailing favor shown to David.”
And again he said in another place, “You have not allowed your holy one to experience decay.”
For David served God's purpose in his own generation and fell asleep. He was gathered to his ancestors and experienced decay.
But the one whom God raised did not experience decay.
Therefore, my brothers, know that forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you through this man.
Through him, everyone who believes is justified from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.
So beware that what is written in the prophets does not come upon you:
“Look, you scoffers! Be amazed and perish! For I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe even if someone told you about it.”
As they were leaving them, the people asked them to speak to them about these things the next Sabbath.
After the assembly was dismissed, many Jews and converts who feared God followed them. They spoke to them and urged them to remain faithful to God's grace.
On the next Sabbath, the whole city gathered to hear the word of God.
When the Jews saw the large crowd, they were filled with jealousy. They opposed what Paul was saying and spoke blasphemously.

But Paul and Barnabas spoke openly: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. But since you reject it and have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, we are now turning to the Gentiles.
For this is what our Lord commanded us, as it is written: ‘I have made you a light to the Gentiles, so that you may bring life to the ends of the earth.’”
When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and praised God. And those who had been appointed to eternal life believed.
The word of the Lord was being proclaimed throughout that whole region.
But the Jews stirred up the city's leaders and the wealthy women who worshiped God with them. They stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their territory.
When they left, they shook the dust off their feet against them and went to the city of Iconium.
The disciples were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.
They came and entered the Jewish synagogue, and spoke with them in such a way that many Jews and Greeks believed.
But the Jews who would not be persuaded stirred up the Gentiles to harm the brothers.
They stayed there a long time, speaking openly about the Lord. He confirmed the message of his grace through the signs and wonders he performed through their hands.
The whole population of the city was divided: some sided with the Jews, while others followed the apostles.
There was a threat against them from the Gentiles and the Jews and their leaders, to mistreat them and stone them.
When they learned of it, they left and took refuge in the cities of Lycaonia—Lystra and Derbe—and the villages around them.
There they preached the good news.
In the city of Lystra, a man was sitting whose feet were disabled. He had been lame from his mother's womb and had never walked.
This man listened to Paul speaking. When Paul saw him and recognized that he had faith to be healed,
He said to him in a loud voice, “I tell you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, stand up on your feet!” He jumped up, stood, and walked.
When the crowd saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices in the local language and said, “The gods have taken human form and come down to us!”
They called Barnabas the lord of the gods, and Paul Hermes, because he took the lead in speaking.
The priest of the lord of the gods, who was outside the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gate of the courtyard where they were staying, and wanted to offer sacrifices to them.
But when Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their clothes and rushed out toward the crowd, shouting

and saying, “Men, what are you doing? We too are human beings, subject to suffering just like you. We bring you the good news so that you may turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the seas and everything in them.
In past generations he allowed all the nations to go their own ways,
yet he did not leave himself without a witness: he did good things for them from heaven, sending them rain, making fruit grow in its seasons, and filling their hearts with food and gladness.”
Even by saying these things, they barely restrained the people from offering sacrifices to them.
But Jews came there from Iconium and Antioch and stirred up the people against them. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead.
The disciples gathered around him, and he got up and entered the city. The next day he left there with Barnabas, and they came to the city of Derbe.
They preached the good news to the people of that city and made many disciples. Then they returned to the city of Lystra, to Iconium, and to Antioch.
They were strengthening the souls of the disciples, urging them to remain in the faith, and telling them, “We must enter the kingdom of God through much suffering.”
They appointed elders for them in every church, fasting and praying with them, and entrusted them to our Lord, in whom they had believed.
After traveling through the region of Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia.
After speaking the word of the Lord in the city of Perga, they went down to Attalia.
From there they traveled by sea and came to Antioch, because it was from there that they had been entrusted to the grace of the Lord for the work they had completed.
When they had gathered the whole church, they recounted everything God had done with them and how he had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
They stayed there with the disciples for a long time.
Some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of the law, you cannot be saved.”
Paul and Barnabas had a great dispute and debate with them. It was decided that Paul and Barnabas, along with some others, should go up to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem about this question.

The church escorted them and sent them on their way. They traveled through all Phoenicia and also through the land of the Samaritans, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers.
When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church, the apostles, and the elders. They told them everything God had done with them.
But some believers who belonged to the teaching of the Pharisees stood up and said, “You must circumcise them and command them to keep the law of Moses.”
The apostles and elders gathered to consider this matter.
After much debate, Simon stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that from the early days God chose that the Gentiles should hear the message of the good news from my own mouth and believe.
God, who knows what is in hearts, testified on their behalf by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us.
He made no distinction between us and them, because he purified their hearts through faith.
Now why are you testing God by putting a yoke on the disciples’ necks that neither our ancestors nor we have been able to bear?
Rather, we believe that we will be saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they will.”
The whole assembly fell silent and listened to Paul and Barnabas as they recounted all the signs and mighty deeds God had done through them among the Gentiles.
After they fell silent, James stood up and said, “Brothers, listen to me.
Simon has told you how God began to choose from among the Gentiles a people for his name.
The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:
‘After these things I will return and raise up David’s tent, which has fallen. I will rebuild what has fallen from it and set it up again,
So that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, along with all the nations over whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who has done all these things.
God's works have been known from eternity.
Therefore I say that we should not trouble those from among the Gentiles who are turning to God.
Instead, we should write to them to keep themselves from the defilement of food sacrificed to idols, from sexual immorality, from strangled animals, and from blood.
For from ancient generations Moses has had people proclaiming him in the synagogues in every city, where they read him every Sabbath.

Then the apostles and elders, together with the whole church, chose men from among them and sent them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas, who is called Barsabbas, and Silas, men who were leaders among the brothers.
They wrote a letter to be delivered by them, as follows: “The apostles, elders, and brothers, to the Gentile brothers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: Greetings.
We have heard that some people went out from us and troubled you with their words and unsettled your souls, saying that you must be circumcised and keep the law. We gave them no such instructions.
For this reason, when we were gathered together, we all decided to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Paul and Barnabas,
men who have put their lives at risk for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have sent Judas and Silas with them, so that they themselves may tell you these same things by word of mouth.
For it was the will of the Holy Spirit, and ours as well, that no further burden should be placed on you beyond these necessary things:

that you keep away from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from strangled animals, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well. Remain steadfast in our Lord.”
Those who were sent came to Antioch, gathered all the people together, and delivered the letter.
When they read it, they rejoiced and were encouraged.
Judas and Silas encouraged the brothers and strengthened them with many words, because they themselves were also prophets.
After they had been there for some time, the brothers sent them off in peace to the apostles.
But Silas wished to remain there.
Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming the word of God along with many others.
After some days, Paul said to Barnabas, "Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed God's message, and see how they are doing."
Barnabas wanted to take John, who was also called Mark.
But Paul did not want to take him with them, because he had left them when they were in Pamphylia and had not gone on with them.
Because of this disagreement, they parted from one another. Barnabas took Mark, and they sailed away to Cyprus.
Paul chose Silas and departed, entrusted by the brothers to the grace of God.
He traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
He arrived at the city of Derbe and at Lystra. There was a disciple there named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Gentile.
All the disciples from Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him.
Paul wanted to take this man with him. He took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in that region, for they all knew that his father was a Gentile.
As they traveled through the cities, they proclaimed and taught the people to observe the instructions that the apostles and elders in Jerusalem had written.
But the churches were being strengthened in the faith and were increasing in number every day.
They traveled through the regions of Phrygia and Galatia, and the Holy Spirit prevented them from speaking the word of God in Asia.
When they came to the region of Mysia, they wanted to go from there to Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.
When they left Mysia, they went down to the region of Troas.
In a vision at night, Paul saw what looked like a Macedonian man standing and pleading with him, saying, “Come to Macedonia and help me.”
When Paul saw this vision, we immediately wanted to leave for Macedonia, because we understood that our Lord had called us to proclaim the good news to them.
We sailed from Troas and headed straight for Samothrace. From there, the next day, we came to the city of Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, which is the chief city of Macedonia and is a colony. We stayed in this city for several days.
On the Sabbath day, we went outside the city gate beside a river, because a house of prayer could be seen there. We sat down and spoke with the women who had gathered there.
There was a woman named Lydia, a seller of purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God. Our Lord opened her heart, and she listened to what Paul was saying.
She and her household were baptized. She pleaded with us, saying, "If you are truly convinced that I have believed in our Lord, come and stay in my house." And she pressed us strongly.
As we were going to the house of prayer, a young woman met us who had a spirit of divination. She earned a great deal of money for her masters through her fortune-telling.
She followed Paul and us, shouting, “These men are servants of God Most High, and they proclaim to you the way of life.”
She kept doing this for many days. Paul became troubled and said to that spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour.
When her masters saw that their hope of profit from her was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace.
They brought them before the magistrates and the city leaders and said, “These men are disturbing our city because they are Jews.
They are proclaiming customs to us that we are not permitted to accept or practice, because we are Romans.”
A large crowd gathered against them. Then the magistrates tore off their clothes and ordered them to be beaten.
After beating them severely, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to guard them securely.
When he received this order, he took them inside and locked them in the inner cell of the prison, fastening their feet in the stocks.
At midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and praising God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, and the foundations of the prison were shaken. Immediately all the doors opened, and everyone's bonds came loose.
When the jailer woke up and saw that the prison doors were open, he took a sword and was about to kill himself, because he thought the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul called out to him in a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here.”
He lit a lamp, rushed inside trembling, and fell at the feet of Paul and Silas.
He brought them outside and said to them, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They said to him, “Believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, and you and your household will be saved.”
They spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his household.
At that very hour of the night, he took them and washed their wounds from the beating. Immediately he and everyone in his household were baptized.
He brought them up into his house and set a meal before them. He and his household rejoiced in their faith in God.
When morning came, the magistrates sent the officers who carried rods to tell the jailer, “Release these men.”
When the jailer heard this, he went in and told Paul the message: “The magistrates have sent orders for you to be released. Now come out and go in peace.”

Paul said to him, “They beat us publicly, in front of everyone, though we had committed no offense and are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison. Now are they sending us out secretly? Certainly not! Let them come themselves and bring us out.”
The officers who carried rods went and reported to the magistrates what had been said to them. When they heard that the men were Roman citizens, they were afraid.
They came to them and begged them to come out and leave the city.
After leaving the prison, they went to Lydia. They saw the brothers there, encouraged them, and departed.
They passed through the cities of Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
As was his custom, Paul went in to them, and for three Sabbaths he spoke with them from the Scriptures,
explaining and showing that the Messiah was destined to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus whom I proclaim to you is the Messiah.”
Some of them believed and joined Paul and Silas, as did many of the Greeks who feared God and quite a few prominent women.

But the Jews became jealous and gathered some wicked men from the city’s marketplaces around them. They formed a large mob and threw the city into turmoil. They came and surrounded Jason’s house, seeking to bring them out from there and hand them over to the mob.

When they did not find them there, they dragged Jason and the brothers who were there before the city officials, shouting, “These are the men who have thrown the whole world into turmoil, and now they have come here too!
This Jason has welcomed them. All these men act against Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, Jesus.”
The city officials and all the people were disturbed when they heard these things.
They took security from Jason and the brothers, and then released them.
The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away that very night to the city of Berea. When they arrived there, they went into the Jewish synagogue.
The Jews there were more open-minded than the Jews in Thessalonica. They gladly listened to the message from them every day, examining the Scriptures to see whether these things were so.
Many of them believed, as did many Greek men and prominent women.
When the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God had been proclaimed by Paul in the city of Berea, they came there too. They did not stop agitating and disturbing the people.
The brothers sent Paul away to go down to the sea, while Silas and Timothy remained in that city.
Those who accompanied Paul went with him as far as the city of Athens. When they left him, they received a letter from him for Silas and Timothy, telling them to come to him quickly.
While Paul was waiting in Athens, he was deeply distressed in his spirit as he saw that the whole city was full of idols.
He spoke in the synagogue with the Jews and those who feared God, and in the marketplace every day with those he encountered.

Philosophers who followed the teaching of Epicurus, and others called Stoics, also debated with him. Some of them said, “What does this babbler want to say?” Others said, “He is proclaiming foreign gods,” because he was proclaiming Jesus and his resurrection to them.
They took hold of him and brought him to the court called the Areopagus, saying to him, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are proclaiming?
For you are planting strange ideas in our ears, and we want to know what these things mean.”
Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who came there concerned themselves with nothing else but telling or hearing something new.
Paul stood in the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every respect you are very devoted to the worship of demons.
For as I walked around and looked at your places of worship, I found an altar on which was written, ‘To the hidden God.’ So the one whom you worship without knowing him is the one I proclaim to you.
For God, who made the world and everything in it, and who is Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by human hands.
Nor is he served by human hands, and he needs nothing, because he himself gives everyone life and breath.
From one blood he made the whole human race to live over the face of the whole earth. By his command he determined their times and set the boundaries of human habitation,
so that they would seek God and search for him, and find him through the things he created. For he is not far from any one of us.
For in him we live and move and exist, as some of the wise men among you have also said: ‘Our lineage comes from him.’
Therefore, since we humans trace our lineage to God, we should not think that the divine nature resembles gold or silver or stone carved by human skill and knowledge.
For God overlooked the times of error, but now he commands all people, everyone everywhere, to repent.
For he has appointed a day on which he will judge the whole earth justly through the man he has chosen, and he has turned everyone toward faith in him by raising him from the dead.
When they heard about the resurrection from the dead, some mocked, while others said, ‘We will hear you about this another time.’
And so Paul left their midst.
Some of them joined him and believed. One of them was Dionysius, one of the judges of the Areopagus, along with a woman named Damaris and others with them.
When Paul left Athens, he came to Corinth.

There he found a Jewish man named Aquila, who was from the region of Pontus. At that time he had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius Caesar had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to them.
Because he practiced the same trade as they did, he stayed with them and worked with them at their trade, for they were tentmakers.
He spoke in the synagogue every Sabbath and sought to persuade the Jews and the Gentiles.

When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul was hard pressed in proclaiming the message, because the Jews were opposing him and speaking blasphemously as he testified to them that Jesus was the Messiah.
He shook out his clothes and said to them, ‘From now on I am innocent. I am going to the Gentiles.’
He left there and entered the house of a man named Titus, who feared God. His house was next to the synagogue.
Crispus, the leader of the synagogue, believed in our Lord, together with his entire household. Many Corinthians heard, believed in God, and were baptized.
The Lord said to Paul in a vision, ‘Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent,
because I am with you, and no one can harm you. I have many people in this city.’
He stayed in Corinth for a year and six months, teaching them the word of God.
When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews gathered together against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
saying, ‘This man persuades people to worship God contrary to the law.’
