When Paul was about to open his mouth and speak, Gallio said to the Jews, "If you were bringing an accusation about something evil, deceitful, or wicked, Jews, I would be obliged to hear you."
‘But if these are disputes about a message, names, and your own law, settle them among yourselves. I do not want to be a judge of these matters.’
And he drove them away from his judgment seat.
All the Gentiles seized Sosthenes, the elder of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But Gallio paid no attention to these things.
After Paul had stayed there many days, he said goodbye to the brothers and sailed for Syria. Priscilla and Aquila went with him. He had his head shaved at Cenchreae because he had taken a vow.
They arrived at Ephesus, and Paul entered the synagogue and spoke with the Jews.
They asked him to stay longer with them, but he would not agree,
saying, “I must by all means celebrate the coming festival in Jerusalem. If God wills, I will return to you again.” He left Aquila and Priscilla in Ephesus.
He sailed and came to Caesarea. He went up and greeted the members of the church, and then went to Antioch.
After spending some time there, he set out and traveled from place to place through the regions of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
A Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was eloquent in speech and well versed in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and was fervent in spirit. He spoke and taught fully about Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak openly in the synagogue. When Aquila and Priscilla heard him, they brought him to their home and explained the way of the Lord to him fully.
When he wanted to go to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he went there, he greatly helped all the believers through grace.
For he argued forcefully against the Jews before the crowds, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul traveled through the upper regions and came to Ephesus. He asked the disciples he found there,
“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They answered him, “We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
He said to them, “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul said to them, “John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, telling them to believe in the one coming after him, that is, Jesus Christ.”
When they heard these things, they were baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Paul laid his hand on them, and the Holy Spirit came upon them. They spoke in various languages and prophesied.
There were twelve men in all.
Paul entered the synagogue and spoke openly for three months, seeking to persuade them about the kingdom of God.

But some of them became stubborn and argumentative and spoke abusively about the way of God before the assembled people. Then Paul withdrew and separated the disciples from them. Every day he spoke with them in the school of a man named Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, until everyone living in Asia, both Jews and Gentiles, had heard the word of the Lord.
God was performing great miracles through Paul,
so that people even brought cloths or aprons from the clothing worn on his body and laid them on the sick. Their diseases left them, and demons also came out.

Some Jews who traveled around invoking oaths over demons also wanted to invoke the name of our Lord Jesus over those who had unclean spirits. They would say, “We command you under oath in the name of Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”
Seven sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva were doing this.
But the evil demon answered them, “I recognize Jesus, and I know Paul, but who are you?”
The man who had the evil spirit leaped on them, overpowered them, and subdued them. They fled from that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the Jews and Gentiles living in Ephesus. Fear fell on them all, and the name of our Lord Jesus Christ was exalted.
Many of those who had believed came and recounted their sins, confessing what they had been doing.
Many sorcerers also gathered their books, brought them, and burned them in front of everyone. They calculated their value, and it amounted to fifty thousand pieces of silver.
In this way, faith in God grew stronger and spread with great power.
When these things were finished, Paul decided to travel throughout Macedonia and Achaia and then go to Jerusalem. He said, “After I have gone there, I must also see Rome.”
He sent two of those who assisted him, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed in Asia for a time.
At that time there was a great disturbance concerning the way of God.
There was a silversmith there named Demetrius who made silver shrines for Artemis and brought considerable profit to his fellow craftsmen.
He gathered all his fellow craftsmen and those who worked with them and said to them, “Men, you know that all our income comes from this work.
You also hear and see that this Paul has persuaded and turned away not only the people of Ephesus but also many throughout Asia, saying that things made by human hands are not gods.

Not only is this business being discredited and brought to nothing, but even the temple of the great goddess Artemis is being regarded as nothing. And the goddess herself, whom all Asia and all the nations worship, is being despised.”
When they heard this, they were filled with rage and shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The whole city was thrown into confusion. They rushed together to the theater, seizing and taking with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonian men who were Paul's traveling companions.
Paul wanted to enter the theater, but the disciples prevented him.
Some of the leaders of Asia, who were his friends, also sent word urging him not to venture into the theater.
The crowds in the theater were in great confusion, and different people were shouting different things. Many of them did not know why they had gathered.
The Jews who were there put forward one of their own, a Jewish man named Alexander. When he stood up, he motioned with his hand and wanted to make a defense before the people.
When they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted with one voice for about two hours, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

The city's chief official quieted them and said, “Men of Ephesus, who among all people does not know that the city of the Ephesians is the priestess of the great Artemis and of her image that came down from heaven?
Since no one can dispute this, you ought to remain calm and do nothing rashly.
For you have brought these men here even though they have neither robbed temples nor insulted our goddess.

If this Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a case against anyone, there is a proconsul in the city. They are competent men. Let them come forward and take their cases against one another to court.
If you seek anything else, it can be settled in the place legally appointed for an assembly.
For even now we are in danger of being accused of rioting, since we cannot give a defense for today's gathering: we assembled without purpose and caused a disturbance without cause.”
After saying this, he dismissed the assembly.
After the disturbance had quieted down, Paul called the disciples, encouraged them, kissed them, and set out for Macedonia.
After traveling through those regions and encouraging them with many words, he came to the land of Greece.
He stayed there for three months. The Jews made a plot against him as he was about to leave for Syria, so he decided to return to Macedonia.

Those who set out with him as far as Asia were Sopater from the city of Berea; Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica; Gaius from the city of Derbe; Timothy from Lystra; and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia.
These men went ahead of us and waited for us at Troas.
After the days of Unleavened Bread, we left Philippi, a city of the Macedonians, and traveled by sea. We reached Troas in five days and stayed there for seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break the Eucharistic bread, Paul spoke with them. Since he was going to leave the next day, he continued speaking until midnight.
There were many burning lamps in the upstairs room where we had gathered.
A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window, listening. He sank into a deep sleep as Paul went on speaking. In his sleep he fell from the third floor and was picked up dead.
Paul went down, threw himself on him, embraced him, and said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is still in him.”
Then he went upstairs, broke bread, and ate. He continued talking until dawn, and then he left to travel overland.
They brought the young man away alive and rejoiced greatly over him.
We went down to the ship and sailed toward Assos, because we were to take Paul aboard there. These were his instructions to us, since he himself was traveling overland.
When we met him at Assos, we took him aboard the ship and came to Mytilene.
From there we sailed the next day to a point opposite the island of Chios. The following day we came to Samos and stayed at Trogyllium. The next day we came to Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he would not be delayed there, because he was hurrying to spend the day of Pentecost in Jerusalem, if possible.
From Miletus he sent for the elders of the church in Ephesus.
When they came to him, he said to them, “You know how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I entered Asia,
serving God with great humility, with tears, and with the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews.
I did not neglect to proclaim to you anything that was beneficial to your souls, and to teach in the streets and in homes.
I testified to Jews and Gentiles about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now I am bound in spirit and am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there.
But in every city the Holy Spirit testifies to me, saying, ‘Imprisonment and suffering await you.’
But I consider my life worth nothing, so that I may finish my race and the ministry I received from our Lord Jesus: to testify to the good news of God’s grace.
And now I know that none of you among whom I traveled proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again.
Therefore I testify to you this very day that I am innocent of the blood of all of you.
For I did not hold back from making known to you the whole will of God.
So watch over yourselves and the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you overseers, to shepherd the church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.
I know that after I leave, fierce wolves will come among you and will not spare the flock.
Even from among your own people, men will arise speaking distorted things to turn the disciples away to follow them.
Therefore stay alert and remember that for three years, night and day, I never stopped warning each one of you with tears.
And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance with all the holy ones.
I did not covet silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands provided for my needs and for those who were with me.

In everything I showed you that we must work hard like this and care for those who are weak, and remember the words of our Lord Jesus, for he said, “The one who gives is more blessed than the one who receives.”
When he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed, and all the people with him.
They all wept bitterly, embraced him, and kept kissing him.
They were especially distressed over what he had said, that they would never see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
We parted from them and sailed straight to the island of Cos. The next day we came to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
There we found a ship going to Phoenicia and boarded it, and sailed [?].
We reached the vicinity of the island of Cyprus, left it on our left, and came to Syria. From there we reached Tyre, for the ship was to unload its cargo there.
When we found disciples there, we stayed with them for seven days. Every day, through the Spirit, they told Paul not to go to Jerusalem.
After these days, we set out to continue our journey. They all accompanied us, with their wives and children, until we were outside the city. They knelt down on the seashore and prayed.
We kissed one another, and we boarded the ship while they returned to their homes.
We sailed from Tyre and came to the city of Acre. We greeted the brothers there and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left and came to Caesarea. We entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed there.
He had four virgin daughters who prophesied.
While we were there for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul's belt, and bound his own feet and hands. He said, “This is what the Holy Spirit says: ‘The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt in this way and hand him over to the Gentiles.’”
When we heard these words, we and the local people begged him not to go to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of our Lord Jesus.”
When he would not be persuaded by us, we stopped and said, “May our Lord's will be done.”
After these days, we got ready and went up to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea also came with us, bringing with them a brother named Mnason, one of the early disciples, who was from Cyprus, so that he could welcome us into his house.
When we came to Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us gladly.
The next day we went with Paul to James, and all the elders were with him.
We greeted them, and Paul recounted to them, one by one, everything God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard this, they praised God and said to him, “You see, our brother, how many tens of thousands in Judea have believed, and all of them are zealous for the law.
But they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews living among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, telling them not to circumcise their sons or follow the customs of the law.
Since, therefore, they will hear that you have come here,
Do what we tell you. We have four men who have made a vow to purify themselves.

Take them and go purify yourself with them. Pay their expenses so that they can shave their heads. Then everyone will know that what has been said about you is false, and that you yourself obey and keep the law.
As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have written that they should keep themselves from food offered in sacrifice, from sexual immorality, from strangled animals, and from blood.”

Then Paul took these men the next day and purified himself with them. He went into the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, until the offering for each one of them was presented.
When the seventh day arrived, Jews from Asia saw him in the temple. They stirred up all the people against him and seized him.

They were shouting and saying, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everywhere against our people, against the law, and against this place. He has even brought Gentiles into the temple and defiled this holy place.”
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they thought he had entered the temple with Paul.
The whole city was in an uproar, and all the people gathered together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and immediately the gates were shut.
While the crowd was trying to kill him, word reached the commander of the cohort that the whole city was in turmoil.
He immediately took the centurion and many soldiers and ran toward them. When they saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander approached him, arrested him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.
People in the crowd were shouting different things about him. Because of their shouting, he could not find out the truth, so he ordered him to be taken into the barracks.
When Paul reached the steps, the soldiers carried him because of the violence of the crowd.
For a large crowd was following him, shouting, “Take him away!”
As Paul was about to enter the barracks, he said to the commander, “If you permit me, I would like to speak with you.” He replied, “Do you know Greek?
Aren’t you that Egyptian who recently stirred up a revolt and led four thousand evildoers out into the wilderness?”
Paul said to him, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a well-known city where I was born. I ask you to let me speak to the people.”
When he gave him permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to them with his hand. When they became quiet, he spoke to them in Hebrew and said:
“Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense I now make before you.
When they heard that he was speaking to them in Hebrew, they became even quieter. And he said to them:

“I am a Jewish man, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel. I was thoroughly instructed in the law of our ancestors, and I was zealous for God, just as all of you are.
I persecuted this Way to the point of death, binding both men and women and handing them over to prison,

as the high priest and all the elders can testify about me. From them I received letters to take to the brothers in Damascus, so that I could also bring those who were there to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.
As I was traveling and approaching Damascus, at midday a great light from heaven suddenly flashed upon me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’
The people who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me.
I said, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ Our Lord said to me, ‘Get up and go to Damascus. There you will be told everything you are commanded to do.’
Since I could not see because of the brilliance of that light, those who were with me took me by the hands, and I entered Damascus.
A man named Ananias, who was righteous according to the law, as all the Jews there testified about him,
came to me and said, ‘Saul, my brother, open your eyes.’ At that very moment my eyes were opened, and I looked at him.
He said to me, ‘The God of our ancestors has appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth.
You will be his witness to all people concerning everything you have seen and heard.
And now, why are you delaying? Get up, be baptized, and be cleansed of your sins, calling on his name.’
I returned and came here to Jerusalem, and I prayed in the temple.
And I saw him in a vision, saying to me, ‘Hurry and leave Jerusalem, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’
I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I used to hand over to prison those who believed in you and beat them in every synagogue.
When the blood of Stephen, your witness, was being shed, I too stood with them and approved of what his killers wanted. I guarded the clothes of those who were stoning him.’
And he said to me, ‘Go, for I am sending you far away to preach to the Gentiles.’”
They listened to Paul up to this statement. Then they raised their voices and shouted, “Rid the earth of someone like this! He does not deserve to live!”
While they were shouting, throwing their clothes, and tossing dust into the air,
the commander ordered that he be brought into the barracks. He ordered that he be interrogated by flogging, so that he could find out why they were shouting against him.
As they stretched him out with straps, Paul said to the centurion standing over him, “Are you allowed to flog a Roman citizen who has not been condemned?”
When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander and said to him, “What are you doing? This man is a Roman citizen!”
The commander came to him and said, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” He said to him, “Yes.”
The commander replied, “I acquired Roman citizenship for a large sum of money.” Paul said to him, “But I was born with it.”
Those who were about to flog him immediately withdrew from him. The commander was afraid when he learned that he was a Roman citizen, because he had bound him.

The next day, wanting to know for certain what accusation the Jews were bringing against him, he released him from his bonds and ordered the chief priests and the entire council of their leaders to come. He took Paul, brought him down, and stood him among them.
Paul looked intently at their council and said, “Brothers, I have lived before God with an entirely good conscience up to this day.”
Ananias the priest ordered those standing beside him to strike Paul on the mouth.
Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there judging me according to the law, yet you break the law by ordering them to strike me!”
Those standing there said to him, “Are you insulting God’s priest?”
Paul said to them, “Brothers, I did not know that he was the priest. For it is written, ‘You must not curse the ruler of your people.’”

When Paul realized that some of the people were Sadducees and some were Pharisees, he called out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. I am on trial because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead.”
When he said this, the Pharisees and Sadducees began to argue with one another, and the people were divided.
For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angels, nor a spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge all of these.

There was a great uproar. Some scribes from the Pharisees’ party stood up and argued with them, saying, “We find nothing wrong with this man. If a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, what is wrong with that?”

When a great disturbance arose among them, the commander was afraid that they might tear Paul apart. He sent word to the Roman soldiers to come, snatch him from among them, and bring him into the barracks.
When night came, our Lord appeared to Paul and said to him, “Take courage, for just as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you are also to testify in Rome.”
When morning came, some of the Jews gathered together and bound themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty men who had bound themselves by oaths to this pledge.
They went to the priests and the elders and said, “We have bound ourselves under a curse not to taste anything until we have killed Paul.”
Now you and the leaders of the council should ask the commander to bring him to you, as though you wanted to investigate his case thoroughly. We are ready to kill him before he reaches you.
But Paul's sister's son heard about this plot, went into the barracks, and told Paul.
Paul sent for one of the centurions and said to him, “Take this young man to the commander, because he has something to tell him.”
The centurion took the young man, brought him to the commander, and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, because he has something to tell you.”
The commander took the young man by the hand, drew him aside, and asked him, “What do you have to tell me?”
The young man said to him, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to their council tomorrow, as though they wanted to learn something more from him.

So do not be persuaded by them. More than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him. They have bound themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed him. They are now ready and waiting for your promise.”
The commander dismissed the young man, ordering him, “Do not let anyone know that you have told me these things.”

He called two centurions and said to them, “Go and get two hundred Roman soldiers ready to go to Caesarea, along with seventy horsemen and two hundred men who throw with their right hands, to leave at the third hour of the night.
Also prepare an animal for Paul to ride, so that they can bring him safely to Felix the governor.”
He wrote a letter and gave it to them. It read as follows:
“Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings.
The Jews seized this man intending to kill him. I intervened with the Roman soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman.
Since I wanted to know the reason for their accusations against him, I brought him down to their council.
I found that they were accusing him over disputes about their law, but there was no charge against him deserving imprisonment or death.
When I was informed of the plot the Jews had made to ambush him, I immediately sent him to you. I also ordered his accusers to come and state their case against him before you. Farewell.”
Then the Romans, as they had been ordered, took Paul by night and brought him to the city of Antipatris.
The next day, the horsemen allowed their fellow soldiers, the infantrymen, to return to the barracks.
They brought him to Caesarea, gave the letter to the governor, and presented Paul before him.
After reading the letter, he asked Paul which province he was from. When he learned that he was from Cilicia,
he said to him, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” He ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod's praetorium.
After five days, Ananias the high priest came down with the elders and an orator named Tertullus, and they brought their complaint against Paul to the governor.
When he was called, Tertullus began accusing him, saying, “We live in great peace because of you, and many improvements have been made for this people through your care.
All of us everywhere acknowledge your kindness, most excellent Felix.
But so that we do not tire you with many words, I ask you to hear us, in our humility, briefly.
For we have found this man to be a corrupting influence who stirs up unrest among all the Jews throughout the world. He is a leader of the teaching of the Nazarenes.
He wanted to defile our temple. When we arrested him, we wanted to judge him according to our law.
But Lysias the commander came and took him from our hands with great force and sent him to you.
He ordered his accusers to come before you. By questioning him, you can learn from him about all these things of which we accuse him.
The Jews themselves also joined in the accusation against him, saying that these things were so.
The governor motioned to Paul to speak. Paul answered, saying, “I know that you have been a judge of this people for many years, and for this reason I gladly make my defense.
You can find out that it has been no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
They did not find me talking with anyone in the temple or gathering a crowd, either in their synagogue or in the city.
Nor can they present proof before you concerning what they now accuse me of.
But I do admit this: according to this teaching they speak of, I worship the God of my ancestors, believing everything written in the Law and the Prophets.
I have hope in God, a hope these people themselves also hold, that there will be a resurrection from the dead of both the righteous and the wicked.
For this reason I also strive always to have a clear conscience before God and before other people.
After many years, I came to my own people to give charitable gifts and present an offering.
These people found me in the temple, ritually purified, without a crowd or a disturbance.
It was some Jews who had come from Asia who caused a disturbance. They ought to have stood with me before you and brought whatever accusation they had.
Or let these people themselves say what wrongdoing they found in me when I stood before their council,
unless it was this one statement that I shouted while standing among them: ‘It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”
But Felix, because he was thoroughly acquainted with this Way, put them off, saying, “When the commander comes, I will hear your case.”
He ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody with some freedom and not to prevent any of his acquaintances from attending to his needs.
A few days later, Felix and his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, sent for Paul and listened to him concerning faith in Christ.
As he spoke with them about righteousness, holiness, and the judgment to come, Felix became frightened and said, “Go away for now. When I have an opportunity, I will send for you.”
For he hoped that Paul would give him a bribe. For this reason he also frequently sent for him, brought him in, and talked with him.
When two years had passed, another governor, called Porcius Festus, came to take his place. But Felix, wanting to do the Jews a favor, left Paul in prison.
When Festus arrived in Caesarea, he went up to Jerusalem three days later.
The chief priests and the Jewish leaders brought their case against Paul to him, and they appealed to him.
They asked him for this favor: that he send for him and bring him to Jerusalem. Meanwhile, they were preparing an ambush along the road to kill him.
Festus answered, “Paul is being kept in Caesarea, and I myself am about to leave.”
“So let those among you who have the authority go down with us and bring charges against the man for any wrongdoing he has committed.”
After staying there eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered Paul to be brought in.
When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem surrounded him, bringing many serious charges against him that they could not prove.
Meanwhile, Paul defended himself, saying that he had committed no offense against the law of the Jews, against the temple, or against Caesar.
But Festus, wanting to gain favor with the Jews, said to Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be tried there before me on these charges?”
Paul answered, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal. This is where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know.”

“If I have committed an offense or done anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is no truth to any of these charges they bring against me, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar.”
Then Festus spoke with his advisers and said, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go.”
After some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice came down to Caesarea to greet Festus.
After they had stayed with him for several days, Festus explained Paul's case to the king, saying, “There is a man whom Felix left in prison.”
“When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews brought their case against him to me and asked me to pass judgment against him in their favor.”

“I told them that it is not the Roman custom to hand anyone over to be killed as a favor before his accuser comes and confronts him face to face, and he is given an opportunity to defend himself against the accusation.”
“When I came here, I made no delay. The next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought before me.”
“His accusers stood up against him, but they could not substantiate any charge of wrongdoing against him of the sort I had expected.”
“Instead, they had certain disputes with him about their religion and about a man named Jesus who had died, whom Paul said was alive.”
“Since I was at a loss as to how to investigate these matters, I asked Paul whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there concerning them.”
“But he asked to be kept in custody for Caesar's judgment, so I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.”
Agrippa said, “I would like to hear this man myself.” Festus said, “Tomorrow you will hear him.”
The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the courtroom with the military commanders and the city's leading men. Festus gave the order, and Paul was brought in.

Festus said, “King Agrippa and all you men who are here with us, the whole Jewish people petitioned me in Jerusalem and here about this man whom you see, shouting that he should no longer be allowed to live.
But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And because he asked to be held for Caesar’s judgment, I ordered that he be sent.

I do not know what to write to Caesar about him. That is why I wanted to bring him before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after his case has been examined, I may find something to write.
For it is not right for us to send a prisoner without writing down his offense.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak on your own behalf.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense, saying:
“King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate that today I am making my defense before you concerning everything of which the Jews accuse me,
especially because I know that you are familiar with all the disputes and laws of the Jews. Therefore I ask you to listen to me patiently.
For the Jews themselves know my way of life from my youth, how I lived from the beginning among my people and in Jerusalem, if they are willing to testify.
They have known me for a long time and know that I lived according to the leading school of the Pharisees.
And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our ancestors.
Our twelve tribes hope to attain this hope through earnest prayers day and night. And it is because of this hope that I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa.
What is your judgment? Should we not believe that God raises the dead?
For I myself had previously made up my mind to do many things against the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

And this is what I did in Jerusalem. I put many of the holy ones in prison, with authority I had received from the chief priests. And when some of them were put to death, I joined those who condemned them.
In every synagogue I tormented them, trying to force them to blaspheme the name of Jesus. I was so filled with anger against them that I even went to other cities to persecute them.
While I was traveling to Damascus for this purpose, with the authority and permission of the chief priests,
at midday on the road, O king, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and everyone who was with me.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in Hebrew, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’
I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And our Lord said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’
And he said to me, ‘Get up and stand on your feet. For I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as a servant and a witness to what you have seen of me and to what you will see of me.
I will rescue you from the Jewish people and from the other nations to whom I am sending you,
to open their eyes so that they may turn from darkness to light and from Satan’s authority to God, and receive forgiveness of sins and a share with those made holy through faith in me.
Therefore, King Agrippa, I did not stand in opposition to the heavenly vision.

Instead, I preached first to those in Damascus, then to those in Jerusalem and in all the villages of Judea. I also preached to the Gentiles that they should repent and turn to God and do deeds worthy of repentance.
Because of these things, the Jews seized me in the temple and wanted to kill me.
But God has helped me to this day, and here I stand, testifying to small and great alike. I say nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets said would happen:
that the Messiah would suffer and be the first to rise from the dead, and that he would proclaim light to the people and to the nations.
As Paul was making his defense in this way, Festus shouted loudly, “You have gone mad, Paul! Your great learning has driven you mad!”
Paul said, “I have not gone mad, most excellent Festus. Rather, I am speaking words of truth and sound judgment.
King Agrippa also knows these things very well, and that is why I speak openly before him. I do not think that any of these things have escaped his notice, for they were not done in secret.
Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe.”
Agrippa said to him, “You are almost persuading me to become a Christian.”
Paul said, “I would pray to God that, whether with little or much, not only you but also everyone listening to me today might become as I am, except for these chains.”
Then the king, the governor, Bernice, and those sitting with them stood up.
After they left there, they spoke with one another, saying, “This man has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
Festus ordered that he be sent to Caesar in Italy. He handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, from the Imperial cohort.

When it was time for us to sail, we boarded a ship from the city of Adramyttium that was going to the region of Asia. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from the city of Thessalonica, boarded the ship with us.
The next day we arrived at Sidon. The centurion treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and rest.
We sailed from there, and because the winds were against us, we went around Cyprus.
We crossed the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia and arrived at Myra, a city in Lycia.
There the centurion found a ship from Alexandria sailing to Italy and put us aboard it.

The ship made slow progress for many days, and we reached a point opposite the island of Cnidus with difficulty. Because the wind would not let us sail straight ahead, we went around Crete, opposite the city of Salmone.
With difficulty, as we sailed around it, we reached a place called Fair Havens. Nearby was a city named Lasea.
We stayed there a long time, until even the Jewish day of fasting had passed, and sailing at sea had become dangerous. Paul advised them,
saying, “Men, I see that our voyage will bring hardship and great loss, not only to our ship’s cargo but also to our own lives.”
But the centurion listened to the pilot and the ship’s owner more than to Paul’s words.
Because that harbor was unsuitable for spending the winter, many of us wanted to sail from there and, if possible, reach a harbor in Crete called Phoenix and spend the winter there. It faced south.
When a south wind blew, they thought they would reach their destination as they wished, and they sailed along the coast of Crete.
A little later, a hurricane-force wind called Euroclydon swept down on us.
The ship was caught and could not hold its course against the wind, so we surrendered to it.
When we passed an island called Cauda, we were barely able to secure the boat.
When we had taken it aboard, we tightened the supports and secured the ship. Because we were afraid of falling into the depths of the sea, we lowered the sail and continued sailing that way.
As a fierce storm battered us, the next day we threw goods into the sea.
On the third day, we threw the ship’s equipment overboard with our own hands.
The storm continued for many days, and neither sun nor moon nor stars could be seen. All hope of surviving was completely gone.
When no one was eating anything, Paul stood among them and said, “Men, if you had listened to me, we would not have sailed from Crete, and we would have been spared this loss and hardship.
Now I advise you not to be anxious, for not one of you will lose your life; only the ship will be lost.
For tonight an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve appeared to me.
He said to me, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. And look, God has granted you as a gift everyone sailing with you.’
So take courage, men, for I trust God that it will happen just as I was told.
But we must be cast ashore on an island.”
After fourteen days of drifting and being tossed about in the Adriatic Sea, around midnight the sailors suspected that they were approaching land.
They lowered anchors and found the depth to be twenty fathoms. They sailed a little farther and found it to be fifteen fathoms.
As we were afraid that we might find ourselves among rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern of the ship and prayed for daylight.
The sailors tried to escape from the ship. They lowered the small boat into the sea, pretending that they would go in it and secure the ship to the shore.
When Paul saw this, he said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay aboard the ship, you cannot survive.”
Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the small boat from the ship and let it drift away.
Until morning came, Paul kept urging them all to take some food, saying to them, “Today marks fourteen days during which you have tasted nothing because of anxiety.”
For this reason, I ask you to eat some food to sustain your lives, for not a hair from the head of any one of you will be lost.
After saying this, he took bread and praised God in front of them all. He broke it and began to eat.
They were all encouraged and took some food.
There were 276 of us aboard the ship.
When they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by taking the wheat and throwing it into the sea.
When daylight came, the sailors did not recognize the land. But they noticed a bay along the shore and were considering whether they could drive the ship into it.
They cut the anchors loose from the ship and left them in the sea. They untied the rudder lashings and raised a small sail to the blowing wind, heading toward the shore.
The ship struck a raised place between two deep parts of the sea and ran aground there. Its bow became stuck on it and would not move, while its stern was broken apart by the force of the waves.
The soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners so that they would not swim away and escape from them.
But the centurion stopped them from doing this because he wanted to save Paul. He ordered those who could swim to swim first and make their way to land.
They brought the rest across on planks and other pieces of wood from the ship. In this way, everyone reached land safely.
Afterward, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The non-Greek-speaking people who lived there showed us great kindness. They lit a fire and invited us all to warm ourselves because of the heavy rain and the cold.
Paul gathered a bundle of sticks and put it on the fire. A viper came out from among them because of the heat of the fire and bit his hand.
When the non-Greek-speaking people saw it hanging from his hand, they said, “Perhaps this man is a murderer. Although he escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”
But Paul shook his hand and threw the viper into the fire, and he suffered no harm.

The non-Greek-speaking people expected him to swell up immediately and fall dead to the ground. But after waiting a long time and seeing that he suffered no harm, they changed what they were saying and said that he was a god.
There were estates in that area belonging to a man named Publius, who was the chief official of the island. He welcomed us gladly into his house for three days.
Publius’s father was sick with fever and intestinal pain. Paul went in to him and prayed, laid his hand on him, and healed him.
After this happened, the other sick people on the island also came to him and were healed.
They honored us greatly, and when we were leaving, they supplied us with provisions.
After three months we departed and sailed in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered on the island. It bore the figurehead of the Twins.
We came to the city of Syracuse and stayed there for three days.
From there we sailed around and reached the city of Rhegium. After one day a south wind blew for us, and two days later we came to Puteoli, a city in Italy.
We found brothers there, and at their invitation we stayed with them for seven days. Then we went to Rome.
When the brothers there heard, they came out to meet us as far as the marketplace called Appii Forum and as far as Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
We entered Rome, and the centurion allowed Paul to stay wherever he wished, with the soldier who guarded him.

After three days Paul sent for the leaders of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, “My brothers, although I had done nothing against the people or the law of my ancestors, I was handed over from Jerusalem as a prisoner into the hands of the Romans.
After questioning me, they wanted to release me, because they found no charge against me deserving death.
But when the Jews opposed me, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—not because I had any accusation to bring against my own people.”
For this reason, I asked you to come so that I could see you and tell you these things, for it is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.
They said to him, “We have received no letter about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers who came from Jerusalem told us anything bad about you.
But we want to hear from you what you think, because we know that this teaching is not accepted by anyone.”

They appointed a day with him, and many gathered and came to him where he was staying. From morning until evening he explained the kingdom of God to them, testifying and trying to persuade them about Jesus from the law of Moses and from the prophets.
Some of them were persuaded by his words, but others were not persuaded.
They left him, disagreeing with one another. Paul said these words to them: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah against your ancestors,
saying, ‘Go to this people and tell them: You will indeed hear but will not understand, and you will see but will not perceive.

For this people’s heart has grown dull. They have made their hearing heavy and have closed their eyes, so that they will not see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn to me, and I would forgive them.’
Therefore, know this: this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen to it.”
When he had said these things, the Jews left, arguing intensely among themselves.
Paul rented a house at his own expense and lived in it for two years. There he welcomed everyone who came to him.
He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught openly about our Lord Jesus Christ, without hindrance.
